pharm: Low molecular weight heparin that potentiates antithrombin-mediated inhibition of activated factor Xa (and to a lesser extent thrombin/factor IIa), reducing thrombin generation and clot formation.
quick: Prophylaxis 3000 anti-Xa IU SC once daily; treatment 8000 anti-Xa IU SC twice daily
LMWHs are preferred anticoagulants when indicated; use per specialist advice
LMWHs are poorly absorbed orally by infant; considered compatible if needed
Caution and consider dose reduction in severe impairment; monitor anti-Xa
Heavy use increases bleeding risk; moderate
Platelet count (HIT), signs of bleeding, renal function, anti-Xa if indicated
summary: Certoparin sodium is a low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) used for the prophylaxis and treatment of venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism). It is given subcutaneously and acts mainly by potentiating antithrombin's inhibition of activated factor Xa. Like other LMWHs, the principal risk is bleeding, and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) can occur. It requires caution in renal impairment, recent surgery/bleeding, and when combined with other antithrombotic drugs. This product is not FDA-approved; see pearls.
indications: Prophylaxis of venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis) in patients at moderate to high risk, including surgical and immobilized medical patients
Treatment of acute deep vein thrombosis (with or without pulmonary embolism)

dosage.n: First dose typically before surgery; continue per risk

dosage.d: 3000 anti-Xa IU once daily (regimen per local protocol)

dosage.n: Overlap with oral anticoagulant until therapeutic

dosage.d: Use with caution; consider dose reduction and anti-Xa monitoring in severe impairment

admin: Administer by deep subcutaneous injection, usually into the abdominal wall, alternating sides
Do not administer by intramuscular injection
Do not expel the air bubble from prefilled syringes before injection
Inject at a 90-degree angle into a skin fold held throughout injection
Do not mix with other injections or infusions
moa: Certoparin is a low molecular weight heparin produced by depolymerization of standard (unfractionated) heparin. It binds to and accelerates the activity of antithrombin III, which then inhibits coagulation factors, predominantly activated factor Xa, with comparatively less inhibition of thrombin (factor IIa) than unfractionated heparin owing to its shorter chain length. The net effect is reduced thrombin generation and fibrin clot formation. Because of its higher anti-Xa to anti-IIa ratio, LMWHs give a more predictable anticoagulant response and require less routine monitoring than unfractionated heparin.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to certoparin, heparin, or other LMWHs
Current or history of immune heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT type II)
Conditions with high bleeding risk (e.g., active peptic ulcer, recent CNS/eye/ear surgery)
relative: Recent surgery, trauma, or lumbar puncture/neuraxial anesthesia
Concomitant antiplatelet or other anticoagulant drugs
monitor: Platelet count (for HIT) before and during therapy
Serum potassium in at-risk patients (heparins can cause hyperkalemia)
Anti-Xa activity in renal impairment, extremes of body weight, or pregnancy

preg: Low molecular weight heparins do not cross the placenta and are generally the anticoagulants of choice in pregnancy when anticoagulation is indicated. Use under specialist guidance; monitor and adjust dosing as pregnancy progresses. Avoid neuraxial anesthesia within the recommended interval after a dose.
lact: Low molecular weight heparins are large molecules that are poorly excreted into breast milk and are not absorbed orally by the infant; they are generally considered compatible with breastfeeding when treatment is required.
renal: Certoparin is partly cleared renally; in severe renal impairment there is a risk of accumulation and increased bleeding. Use with caution, consider dose reduction, and monitor anti-Xa activity and for signs of bleeding.
hepatic: Use with caution in severe hepatic impairment because of impaired synthesis of clotting factors and increased bleeding risk; monitor closely.

major: Other anticoagulants (vitamin K antagonists, DOACs, unfractionated heparin, fondaparinux, thrombolytics) - additive bleeding risk
Antiplatelet agents (aspirin, clopidogrel, ticagrelor, NSAIDs, dipyridamole) - increased bleeding risk
moderate: Drugs that increase serum potassium or affect aldosterone (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics) - additive hyperkalemia risk
Systemic corticosteroids - increased risk of GI bleeding
minor: Drugs that affect platelet function may modestly add to bleeding risk
interactions.alcohol: Heavy alcohol use can increase bleeding risk and should be limited.
interactions.diagnostics: Can cause a transient rise in liver transaminases; can prolong activated partial thromboplastin time at higher doses and may cause hyperkalemia.

serious: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) with or without thrombosis

monitoring: Platelet count before starting and periodically (to detect HIT)
Clinical signs of bleeding and hemoglobin/hematocrit
Renal function, especially in elderly and at-risk patients
Serum potassium in patients at risk of hyperkalemia
Anti-factor Xa activity when monitoring is indicated (renal impairment, obesity, pregnancy)
counsel: This medicine is injected under the skin; learn the correct injection technique if self-administering
Report unusual bruising, nosebleeds, blood in urine or stool, black stools, or prolonged bleeding
Seek urgent care for severe headache, sudden weakness, or numbness, which may signal serious bleeding
Tell your doctor before any surgery, dental work, or spinal/epidural procedure
Avoid other blood thinners and NSAIDs unless approved by your doctor
pk: Anticoagulant (anti-Xa) effect within 1-2 hours of subcutaneous dose
Peak anti-Xa activity approximately 3-4 hours after subcutaneous injection
Anti-Xa effect persists for much of a 24-hour interval at prophylactic doses
Store at controlled room temperature; do not freeze; protect from light
pearls: Not FDA-approved; used in Europe and elsewhere - guidance is based on EMA/SmPC and manufacturer information
Check baseline and periodic platelet counts to detect heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)
Avoid neuraxial (spinal/epidural) procedures within the recommended dosing interval to reduce spinal hematoma risk
Accumulates in renal impairment - use caution, reduce dose, and consider anti-Xa monitoring
Protamine only partially reverses LMWH anticoagulant effect
missed: If a scheduled dose is missed, give it as soon as remembered on the same day; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the regular schedule. Do not give a double dose to make up for a missed one. Keep a record of injection times.
overdose: Overdose can cause hemorrhagic complications. Stop the drug and provide supportive care. Protamine sulfate partially neutralizes the anticoagulant effect of LMWH (it neutralizes the anti-IIa activity completely but only partly reverses anti-Xa activity); the dose of protamine is based on the amount of certoparin given. Monitor for bleeding and replace blood/clotting factors as needed.
